[MUQATIL:7:190-197/r10] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The challenge is to ask the idols to respond by proving they are gods if their worshippers are truthful.
[MUQATIL:7:190-197/r9] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Those worshipped besides God are idols, servants like their worshippers, and not gods.
[TAB-FULL:v10p635/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Addressing idol worshippers, al-Ṭabarī says the idols they call and worship as gods are servants owned by their Lord, just as humans are His servants; worshipping them is associating partners and disbelief.
[TAB-FULL:v10p635/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | If idols cannot hear a caller and answer, they cannot harm or benefit; only one who hears requests and can reward, punish, or help can truly bring benefit or harm.
[IBNABIHATIM:v5p1636/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | On the Resurrection, the sun and moon and their worshipers will be brought before God, and the worshipers will be told to call upon them.
[IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p269/r5] IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB, d. 392 · author | holds | Saʿīd ibn Jubayr reads عبادا أمثالكم in the accusative; Ibn Jinnī treats إن as a negative particle like ما, though he calls this weak because إن lacks ما’s restricted negation and licensing.
[IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p269/r6] IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB, d. 392 · author | holds | On Saʿīd’s reading, the idols are stone or wood, less than their rational worshippers; the common nominative reading calls them servants because they too are created, like all created things that glorify God. | mentions 55:6, 17:44
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p528/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · المفسرون | reports | The exegetes identify those invoked besides God as idols.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p528/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ata reports from Ibn Abbas that those invoked are angels.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p528/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | rejects | The angel interpretation is weak: the polytheists of that time worshipped idols, and the next verse describes beings with no walking legs or grasping hands; this points to inanimate idols. | mentions 7:195
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p528/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The invocation may mean worship or naming them as gods, and من دون الله means other than God. | mentions 7:191
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p529#2/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says to worship the idols and ask whether they can reward or repay you.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p529#2/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أهل المعاني | reports | The people of meaning say the challenge is to seek benefits and removal of harms from the idols, which is impossible; the imperative lām is for incapacitation.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p529#2/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says the condition challenges claims that idols give benefits, reward, intercession, or support.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p529#2/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · صاحب النظم | reports | The صاحب النظم reads إن interrogatively, with an implied hamza: the verse denies that idols are servants like humans, who have reason, hearing, and sight, then challenges their worshippers to summon them; 64:6 and 26:22 exemplify questions without an expressed hamza. | mentions 64:6, 26:22
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p529#2/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · صاحب النظم | reports | He argues that this is not a plain assertion: it rhetorically belittles the idols as inferior even to human servants before the following challenge tests their claimed power.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p529/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الكلبي | reports | Al-Kalbi glosses the idols as owned beings like you.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p529/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash says they are servants in the sense that they are subdued under God's command; the term for slave likewise reflects subjection.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p529/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · قطرب | reports | Qutrub glosses them as created beings like you.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p529/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو بكر بن الأنباري | reports | Ibn al-Anbari says the idols are grammatically treated like people because worshippers claim they reason, discern, harm, and benefit; this licenses الذين, masculine plural forms, and عباد, unlike ordinary inanimate objects.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:7:193-196/r2] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | Those invoked besides God are idols, created and owned beings.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:7:193-196/r3] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | The challenge asks whether idols can reward, requite, or benefit their worshippers, exposing claims that they provide benefit, reward, or intercession.
[JISHUMI:v4p2813/r15] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Duʿāʾ is a request for an action in a specified verbal form, which may be an imperative, a prohibition, or a statement such as ‘May God forgive him.’
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p315/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Those invoked besides God are the idols.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p315/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Calling them servants like you means they are owned as you are; alternatively, they are subjected to whatever is done with them.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p315/r3] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · مقاتل | reports | Muqatil says the phrase refers to angels, addressing people who worshipped angels; the author says the first interpretation is sounder.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p315/r4] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The challenge means invoke them to answer if you are truthful that they are gods.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p315/r5] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas glosses invoke them as worship them: will they reward or save you if you truly expect benefit from them?
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p178/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | تدعون means worshipping them and naming them gods besides God.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p178/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The phrase mocks the idols: even if they were living and rational, they would merely be servants like their worshippers, with no superiority; the next questions deny they can act like people.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p178/r3] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · قيل | reports | Another interpretation takes عباد أمثالكم to mean that the idols are owned or subjected, as you are.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p178/r4] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿīd b. Jubayr reads إن lightly and عبادا in the accusative: ‘Those you invoke are not servants like you’; إن works like the negative ما of Hijazi Arabic.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p488#2/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · جمهور الناس | reports | The majority read inna with a geminated nūn and ʿibād in the nominative; the address belittles idols as created, material bodies that are themselves subject to worship or ownership.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p488#2/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · مقاتل | reports | Maqātil says the verse addresses a group of Khuzaʿa who worshipped angels, informing them that angels are servants like them, not gods.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p488#2/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿīd b. Jubayr reads the nūn of in lightly and puts ʿibādan and amthālakum in the accusative: in means “not,” denying that idols are servants like humans.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p488#2/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | On Saʿīd b. Jubayr’s reading, the idols are less and baser than humans because they are inert and cannot understand or reason.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p488#2/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · سيبويه | reports | Sībawayhi says in meaning mā is too weak to govern the predicate, so it remains nominative; this is the grammatical form he considers correct for the reading.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p488#2/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أبو العباس المبرد | reports | Al-Mubarrad permits in when it means mā to govern like mā and put its predicate in the accusative.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p488#2/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisāʾī says in meaning mā only occurs with illā, as in 67:2. | mentions 67:2
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p488#2/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The command is a test: call the idols, and if they do not answer, that confirms the description just given.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p489/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Saʿīd b. Jubayr’s reading, understood as negation, entails that idols are not servants like human beings.
[TABRISI:7:194-195/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | This second command to invoke them concerns asking the idols for help in urgent needs and for removal of harm.
[TABRISI:7:194-195/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The imperative lām is a challenge meant to expose and ridicule their inability, like the demand “bring your proof if you are truthful.” | mentions 27:64
[TABRISI:7:194-195/r12] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas glosses the challenge as “worship them”: will they reward or requite you if you truly expect benefit, reward, intercession, or support?
[TABRISI:7:194-195/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan says the idols are created beings like their worshippers.
[TABRISI:7:194-195/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · الكلبي | reports | Al-Kalbi interprets them as owned beings like their worshippers.
[TABRISI:7:194-195/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash says they resemble people in being subjected and subdued under God's command; they cannot resist what God wills, so they are servants in the sense of being humbled.
[TABRISI:7:194-195/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The root sense of servitude is subduing; the idols' inability to resist God's will makes them servants in the sense of being subdued. | mentions 26:22
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p306/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Those invoked apart from God are idols.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p306/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The idols are called servants like people because they too are subjected and humbled to God's command.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p306/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The challenge says to call on them despite their being inanimate, as explained under the earlier phrase that they are created. | mentions 7:191

[RAZI-FULL:v15p74/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Because idolaters claim idols benefit and harm, the verse addresses them as if they believe idols intelligent; masculine الذين and فليستجيبوا match that presumed belief.
[RAZI-FULL:v15p75/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Rāzī reads the concession sarcastically: even if idols were living and rational, they would be fellow servants, so humans have no basis for making them gods; the next verse refutes even this concession. | mentions 7:195
[RAZI-FULL:v15p75/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Calling the idols means asking them to bring benefits or remove harms; the imperative lām in “let them respond” is a challenge showing their incapacity and unsuitability for worship.
[RAZI-FULL:v15p75/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The condition challenges the idolaters to prove their claim that the idols are gods deserving worship.

[RAZI-FULL:v15p75/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Since three conclusive proofs show idols are unfit for worship, a rational person should turn only to the God who is powerful, knowing, living, wise, and able to harm and benefit.
[QURTUBI-FULL:7:194-196/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Here tadʿūna means that the polytheists worship the idols.
[QURTUBI-FULL:7:194-196/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿīd ibn Jubayr reads inna lightly with kasra and reads ʿibādan and amthālakum in the accusative.
[QURTUBI-FULL:7:194-196/r12] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | On Saʿīd ibn Jubayr’s reading, idols are stone and wood, so people worship what is nobler than themselves.
[QURTUBI-FULL:7:194-196/r13] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النحاس | rejects | Al-Naḥḥās rejects this reading: it conflicts with the codex; Sibawayh favors a nominative predicate after inna used as mā; al-Kisāʾī says inna rarely means mā without an affirmative. | mentions 35:40

[QURTUBI-FULL:7:194-196/r15] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قيل | reports | An ellipsis means: invite them to follow you and let them respond if you are right that they are gods.
[QURTUBI-FULL:7:194-196/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قيل | reports | An alternative takes it to mean that they call the idols gods.
[QURTUBI-FULL:7:194-196/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Min dūni Allāh means other than God.
[QURTUBI-FULL:7:194-196/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The idols are called servants because they are owned by God and subjected to Him.
[QURTUBI-FULL:7:194-196/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan says the idols are created beings like you.

[QURTUBI-FULL:7:194-196/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The challenge is to ask the idols for benefit or harm.
[QURTUBI-FULL:7:194-196/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The challenge tests their claim that worshipping idols brings benefit.
[QURTUBI-FULL:7:194-196/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says the command means worship them.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:7:194/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Calling them means worshipping them and naming them gods.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:7:194/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The idols are servants like humans in being owned and subjected.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:7:194/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | If the idols really are gods, call them and see whether they can answer.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:7:194/r4] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Alternatively, carved in human form, their utmost status would be living rational beings like their worshippers, who are no more entitled to worship one another.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p51#4/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | «Those you call» means those you worship and name as gods.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p51#4/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The idols are servants like their worshippers: created, owned, and controlled.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p51#4/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Call on them to bring benefit or avert harm; let them answer if you truly believe they are gods.
[QASHANI:7:194/r1] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Whatever is invoked besides God, human or otherwise, is a servant like the worshippers, equally unable and without independent effect.

[QASHANI:7:194/r3] QASHANI, d. 736 · النبي عليه الصلاة والسلام | reports | The Prophet tells Ibn Abbas to guard God, ask and seek help only from God, and know that no community can benefit or harm except by what God has written.
[QASHANI:7:194/r4] QASHANI, d. 736 · النبي عليه الصلاة والسلام | reports | The same report says all benefit and harm are predetermined, with the pens lifted and pages dried.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p249/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | This sentence confirms the preceding argument that the idols cannot cause benefit or harm.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p249/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The beings called gods are themselves servants of God, who created them and their worshippers.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p249/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan explains their likeness as being owned by God.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p249/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · التبريزي | reports | Al-Tabrīzī explains their likeness as being created.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p249/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مقاتل | reports | Muqātil says this addresses a Khuzāʿa group that worshipped angels; God clarifies that they are servants like their worshippers, not gods.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p249/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī reads the comparison as mockery: even if idols were alive and rational, they would still be servants like their worshippers, with no superiority.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p249/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abū Ḥayyān rejects al-Zamakhsharī's claim that the following question cancels the likeness: likeness in creation or ownership remains, while the question belittles the idols' missing organs and uses.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p249/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The question about organs cannot invalidate God's earlier statement; that would make one of two divine reports false, which is impossible.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p249/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Lacking useful organs does not negate likeness in being created or owned and subdued; the question instead shows idols are inferior to humans.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p250/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن جبير | reports | Ibn Jubayr reads a light in and the accusative ʿibādan amthālakum.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p250/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · المفسرون | reports | Commentators parse this as negative in working like the Ḥijāzī mā: it raises the subject and puts the predicate ʿibādan amthālakum in the accusative, denying likeness to humans.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p250/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The Kufans, Ibn al-Sarrāj, al-Fārisī, and Ibn Jinnī permit negative in to govern like mā; al-Farrāʾ and most Basrans reject that usage, while reports differ about Sībawayh and al-Mubarrad.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p250/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Abū Ḥayyān says the correct position is that in can work like mā; this is a usage attested in both prose and poetry.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p250/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | He rejects the negative-in parsing because it denies likeness, contradicting the majority reading that affirms it and implying incompatible divine reports.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p250/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · النحاس | reports | Al-Naḥḥās objects to the reading because it differs from the codex consonantal text, conflicts with Sībawayh's preferred nominative predicate, and conflicts with al-Kisāʾī's account of negative in.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p250/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abū Ḥayyān answers that the reading is transmitted from a distinguished Successor, its orthographic difference is slight and perhaps reflects Rabīʿa spelling, and the accounts of Sībawayh and al-Kisāʾī are disputed.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p251/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Another parsing takes lightened in as still emphatic and governing like full inna, allowing ʿibādan as its accusative predicate.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p251/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Abū Ḥayyān compares the challenge to Abraham's question to his father about worshipping what cannot hear, see, or help. | mentions 19:42
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p251/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · عمر بن أبي ربيعة | reports | A line by ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa supplies an example of an accusative predicate after inna.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p251/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · جماعة من النحاة | reports | Some grammarians allow accusative predicates with inna and its sisters, citing clear poetic evidence; their opponents interpret those examples differently.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p251/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Alternatively, opponents can treat the ac

cusative as an omitted verb, as in the poem about wishing youth's days back; this keeps both readings equivalent in meaning.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p251/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Another reading lightens in and puts ʿibādan in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative from an omitted pronoun in the relative clause; amthālakum is nominative predicate.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p251/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Whether the likeness is in creation or ownership, such beings cannot be gods.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p251/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The imperative to call them is a challenge: test by invoking them whether they can answer; they cannot.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p251/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Being truthful means that the idolaters' claim that their gods are divine and deserve worship is true.
[SAMIN-DURR:7:194#2/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الشيخ | reports | The Shaykh parses light إن as operative and cites إن حراسنا أسدا as evidence that it can put both nominal parts in the accusative; he also invokes the reading إن كلا and a poetic example interpreted as ترى رواجعا. | mentions 11:111
[SAMIN-DURR:7:194#2/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Al-Samīn inventories three parses for the reading: negative إن governing like ما, light operative إن governing both accusatives, or accusatives governed by an implied verb that supplies the predicate's meaning.
[SAMIN-DURR:7:194#2/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Al-Samīn notes that the operative-light-إن parse rests on two contested doctrines: applying light إن is rare, and إن and its sisters governing both parts is a weaker grammatical position.
[SAMIN-DURR:7:194#2/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · بعضهم | reports | Some read light إن, accusative عباد, and nominative أمثالكم; they treat إن as ungoverned, الذين as subject, عباد as a circumstantial accusative of its omitted object pronoun, and أمثالكم as predicate, meaning the idols are created and owned like their worshippers.
[SAMIN-DURR:7:194#2/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Al-Samīn says making the relative pronoun accusative in that last parse is weak because governing with light إن was already described as rare.
[SAMIN-DURR:7:194#2/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abū al-Baqāʾ also transmits a fourth reading, geminated إن with عباد accusative and أمثالكم nominative, parsed like the preceding variant.
[SAMIN-DURR:7:194/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The standard reading has إن geminated, with the relative pronoun as its subject and عباد as its predicate.
[SAMIN-DURR:7:194/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿīd ibn Jubayr reads إن lightly with عباد and أمثالكم in the accusative.
[SAMIN-DURR:7:194/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو الفتح ابن جني | reports | Ibn Jinnī and others parse the light إن in Saʿīd's reading as a negative particle working like Hijazi ما; this is held by al-Kisāʾī and most Kufans except al-Farrāʾ, and by Basrans Ibn al-Sarrāj, al-Fārisī, and Ibn Jinnī, while reports differ about Sibawayh and al-Mubarrad.
[SAMIN-DURR:7:194/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Al-Samīn says the negative particle's accusative government is established in prose and poetry, citing an unattested-by-name poetic line with مستوليا.
[SAMIN-DURR:7:194/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Critics say the negative reading contradicts the canonical affirmation that the idols are servants like people; the answer is that humans can harm and benefit whereas inert idols cannot, so the reading reinforces the canonical meaning a fortiori.
[SAMIN-DURR:7:194/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو جعفر | rejects | Abū Jaʿfar rejects the variant for conflicting with the muṣḥaf consonantal form, for Sibawayh's preference to leave light إن ungoverned, and because al-Kisāʾī requires an affirmative after إن.
[SAMIN-DURR:7:194/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الشيخ | rejects | The Shaykh answers that Rabiʿa could write accusative nunation without an alif at pause, so the reading need not conflict with the muṣḥaf form; al-Samīn also says the claimed restrictions about Sibawayh and al-Kisāʾī are disputed or unestablished.
[SAMIN-DURR:7:194/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | Al-Samīn dismisses al-Naḥḥās's objection as slight orthographic variance and says the reports about Sibawayh are disputed and the restriction attributed to al-Kisāʾī is not established.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p529#2/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The idols are creatures like their worshippers; humans are more complete because they hear, see, and act, while idols do none of these things.
[BURHAN:v1p118/r12] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Al-Naḥl says “those they call upon besides God,” while al-Aʿrāf uses “besides Him.”
[BURHAN:v4p54/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Calling the alleged partners God's partners reflects the polytheists' claim, not a divine affirmation of partnership. | mentions 2:165
[BIQAI-FULL:v3p170/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The invocation is bound to worship: the polytheists invoke their idols as objects of worship, and calling is inseparable from the one worshipped.
[BIQAI-FULL:v3p170/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | reports | Alternatively, invocation is used for worship to show that one incapable of being invoked cannot rightly be worshipped.
[BIQAI-FULL:v3p170/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The idols are powerless servants like their worshippers, especially unable to meet the Qur’an’s challenge; humans surpass them in life and reason, while a true deity cannot be like a worshipper.
[BIQAI-FULL:v3p170/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The challenge is to call them to anything and see if they answer clearly, produce a comparable surah, or provide any benefit; a true god would answer a devotee.
[BIQAI-FULL:v3p170/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿīd ibn Jubayr reads إن lightly and عبادا أمثالكم with the accusative, treating إن as a negative particle that raises its noun and sets its predicate in the accusative.
[BIQAI-FULL:v3p170/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | reports | Grammarians dispute whether إن may work like الحجازية ما: al-Kisāʾī, most Kufans, Ibn al-Sarrāj, al-Fārisī, and Ibn Jinnī allow it; al-Farrāʾ and most Basrans reject it, with reports differing on Sibawayh and al-Mubarrad.
[BIQAI-FULL:v3p170/r7] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Biqāʿī holds that this grammatical use of إن is a documented language found in both verse and prose.
[BIQAI-FULL:v3p170/r8] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The negative reading need not conflict with the familiar affirmative: affirmation concerns shared incapacity, while denial concerns equality, since people exceed idols in other capacities.
[BIQAI-FULL:v3p170/r9] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī resolves the readings by taking the affirmative as concessive and the negation as the literal truth.
[DURR-FULL:v3p626/r8] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿīd b. Jubayr reports that the sun and moon will be brought before God along with those who worshipped them, and they will be told to call on them if they are truthful.
[ITQAN:v2p449#4/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | إن with kasra and no shadda can be a negative particle, entering nominal or verbal clauses; grammarians dispute whether it is restricted to constructions with إلا or لما. | mentions 9:32, 58:2, 10:18, 4:117, 86:4
[ITQAN:v2p449#4/r5] ITQAN, d. 911 · الكسائي والمبرد | reports | Al-Kisaʾi and al-Mubarrad allow negative إن to govern like ليس and apply that parsing to Saʿid ibn Jubayr's reading of this verse.
[BURSEVI:v3p226/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The objects worshipped besides God are idols called gods, yet are owned, governed, and unable to bring benefit or harm.
[BURSEVI:v3p226/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · الحدادي | reports | Al-Haddadi says the idols are called servants because their makers fashioned them in human form.
[BURSEVI:v3p226/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The challenge is to call the idols for benefit or removal of harm; the command that they respond is a taunt meant to show their incapacity.
[BURSEVI:v3p226/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Their claim is that the idols can do what their worshippers cannot; the challenge exposes that claim as false.
[ALUSI-FULL:v9p143#4/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The verse confirms the preceding point that the idols do not follow their worshippers’ calls. | mentions 7:193
[ALUSI-FULL:v9p143#4/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The replies say the construction occurs in Arabic; the readings need not conflict because one can affirm likeness in one respect while the other denies it wholly or in another respect.
[ALUSI-FULL:v9p143#4/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Another parsing treats the light إن as a weakened heavy إن that unusually governs both accusatives; because this is rare and weak, some leave إن ungoverned and supply an omitted predicate.
[ALUSI-FULL:v9p143#4/r12] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | A recited heavy anna has ʿibādan as a circumstantial accusative from the omitted pronoun and amthālukum as its nominative predicate.
[ALUSI-FULL:v9p143#4/r13] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | A further transmitted form has amthālukum nominative with the light reading and ʿibād accusative, parsed as a circumstantial accusative plus predicate.

[ELMALILI:7:190-198/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The intended rebuke is that the polytheists themselves resemble the inert idols they worship.
[ELMALILI:7:190-198/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The idols neither follow a call to guidance nor answer prayers, so seeking their help is futile.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v9p220/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | On the first reading of the preceding address, this begins a new address to the polytheists; emphasis counters their denial that idols share their servitude, and the wording shifts from third person to direct address. | mentions 7:193
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v9p220/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The relative phrase refers to idols and alerts the polytheists that their invocation is misguided; ʿAbda ibn al-Ṭabīb’s similar relative phrasing is cited as a parallel.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v9p220/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | If the prior address was to the Prophet and Muslims, this sentence independently turns to address the polytheists. | mentions 7:193

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v9p220/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | ʿAbd originally means a person owned rather than free, then Arabic extended it to any creature, as in the cited Qurʾanic uses. | mentions 2:178, 19:93

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v9p220/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · صاحب الكشاف | reports | Al-Kashshāf treats calling idols servants as mockery of the polytheists: even if idols were alive and rational, they would still be creatures like their worshippers. | mentions 7:195
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v9p220/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | prefers | Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers a metaphorical usage by assumed concord: since worshippers and idols are alike as created beings, he calls their counterparts servants as worshippers are servants of God.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v9p221/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The command to call the idols is a challenge: invocation is possible but their response is not, exposing both their impotence and the worshippers’ inability to establish their claim; 35:14 makes the same point. | mentions 35:14

[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-3-surah-araf-07:p137/r7] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | People receive every favor from God yet thank others and associate partners incapable of benefiting or harming them.
